groups.instructionTh: ฟังบทสนทนาต่อไปนี้ แล้วตอบคำถาม 5 ข้อ (บทสนทนาจะเล่นเป็นเสียง)
groups.title: A meeting with a thesis supervisor

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Come in, have a seat. I've had a chance to go through your second chapter.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Thanks for getting to it so quickly. I wasn't sure whether the structure was working.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: The structure's mostly fine. My main concern is the sampling. You interviewed forty-two street vendors, but thirty of them work at a single night market.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: I know. The other markets were much harder to get access to, and I was running out of time before the rainy season.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: That's understandable, but an examiner will pounce on it. You either need to widen the sample or narrow your claims.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Narrowing the claims feels like giving up on the comparative angle, though.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Not necessarily. You could present the night market as an in-depth case study and treat the other twelve interviews as a contrast group. That's a perfectly respectable design.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: So I'd reframe the research questions rather than go back and collect more data?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Exactly. More fieldwork now would push your submission back at least a semester, and your scholarship runs out in May.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Right. What about the literature review? I felt it was a bit thin.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Thin isn't really the problem. It reads like a catalogue. You summarise one study after another without showing how they relate to each other. Group them by argument, not by author.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: That makes sense. Should I send you the revised chapter before the progress committee meets?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Please do, but give me at least ten days. The committee meets on the fourteenth, so aim for the first few days of the month.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Okay. I'm also going to email Dr. Somsri to ask whether she'd join the committee as the external member.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Good idea. Just copy me in, so she knows I've approved the request.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Will do. Thanks, this was much less painful than I expected.

items.stem: What is the supervisor's main concern about the chapter?
options: Most of the interviews come from one location.
The interviews were held during the rainy season.
Forty-two interviews are too few overall.
items.explanationTh: อาจารย์บอกว่า "My main concern is the sampling" เพราะผู้ให้สัมภาษณ์ 30 จาก 42 คนอยู่ที่ตลาดกลางคืนแห่งเดียว ส่วนโครงสร้างนั้น "mostly fine"

items.stem: What does the supervisor recommend the student do about her sample?
options: Interview vendors at several more markets.
Treat it as a case study with a comparison group.
Remove the twelve interviews from other markets.
Delay her submission until next semester.
items.explanationTh: อาจารย์เสนอให้ "present the night market as an in-depth case study and treat the other twelve interviews as a contrast group" คือปรับกรอบเป็นกรณีศึกษาพร้อมกลุ่มเปรียบเทียบ ไม่ต้องเก็บข้อมูลเพิ่ม

items.stem: Why does the supervisor advise against collecting more data?
options: Fieldwork is not allowed during the rainy season.
It would delay her beyond the end of her funding.
The committee has already approved the design.
The new data could not be compared with the old.
items.explanationTh: อาจารย์บอกว่าการเก็บข้อมูลเพิ่ม "would push your submission back at least a semester" และ "your scholarship runs out in May" แปลว่าจะเลยระยะเวลาทุน

items.stem: What does the supervisor say about the literature review?
options: It should be cut to half its length.
It discusses far too few studies on the topic.
It lists studies without linking them together.
It relies too heavily on one author.
items.explanationTh: อาจารย์บอกว่าปัญหาไม่ใช่ความบาง แต่ "reads like a catalogue" สรุปงานทีละชิ้น "without showing how they relate to each other"

items.stem: What will the student most likely do about Dr. Somsri?
options: Arrange to meet her before the fourteenth.
Email her and include the supervisor in the message.
Send her the revised second chapter.
Ask the supervisor to contact Dr. Somsri directly.
items.explanationTh: นักศึกษาจะอีเมลถึง Dr. Somsri และอาจารย์ขอให้ "copy me in" ซึ่งเธอตอบว่า "Will do" จึงจะส่งอีเมลโดยสำเนาถึงอาจารย์ด้วย

groups.instructionTh: ฟังบทสนทนาต่อไปนี้ แล้วตอบคำถาม 5 ข้อ (บทสนทนาจะเล่นเป็นเสียง)
groups.title: Booking a field station

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Good morning, Saen Khlong Field Station, bookings office.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Hello. I'm calling from the marine ecology course at Phrayathep University. We'd like to bring eighteen students for three nights in late January.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Late January is quite busy. Which dates exactly?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: We'd arrive on the twenty-second and leave on the twenty-fifth.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: I'm afraid our dormitory only sleeps sixteen. We could put two people in the staff cottage, but that costs an extra four hundred baht per person per night.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: That's fine. The department is covering accommodation anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Good. Now, are you planning to go out onto the mudflats?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Yes, that's really the whole point. We're sampling crab burrows along fixed transects.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Then I should warn you that the low tides that week fall very early, around half past five in the morning. If you miss that window, the flats won't be safe again until the evening.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Half past five? Oh, my students will be thrilled.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: I'm sure they will. Also, everyone who goes onto the flats has to attend our safety induction on the first evening. No exceptions, not even for teaching staff.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Understood. Do we need to bring our own boots?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: We lend boots, but the large sizes run out quickly. Anyone who takes a size forty-four or above should bring a pair.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Noted. And is there anywhere we can process samples?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: There's a wet lab with two microscopes. If you need more, you'll have to bring them, and the lab closes at nine sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Perfect. Could you send me something in writing?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: I'll email you a provisional booking today. It only becomes confirmed once we receive a deposit, which needs to reach us within two weeks.

items.stem: Why is the man calling the field station?
options: To arrange a safety induction for his staff.
To ask about the times of the low tides.
To reserve places for a class field trip.
To check whether the station lends boots.
items.explanationTh: จุดประสงค์หลักอยู่ที่ประโยคแรก "We'd like to bring eighteen students for three nights" คือโทรมาจองที่พักสำหรับทริปภาคสนาม ส่วนเรื่องน้ำลง การอบรม และรองเท้าบูทเป็นรายละเอียดที่ผู้หญิงแจ้งระหว่างคุย ไม่ใช่เหตุผลที่โทรมา

items.stem: What problem does the woman mention about the group?
options: The department must pay for the cottage first.
The staff cottage has already been booked.
The group is too small for a group rate.
Not all of the students can sleep in the dormitory.
items.explanationTh: หอพัก "only sleeps sixteen" แต่มานักศึกษา 18 คน จึงต้องให้ 2 คนไปพักที่บ้านพักเจ้าหน้าที่

items.stem: What does the man imply when he talks about his students and the early tide?
options: The students are looking forward to the safety induction.
The students will not be pleased about getting up so early.
The students have asked to work in the mornings.
The early tide fits neatly into the students' timetable.
items.explanationTh: "my students will be thrilled" เป็นการพูดประชด หลังได้ยินว่าต้องลงพื้นที่ตอนตีห้าครึ่ง จึงหมายความว่านักศึกษาคงไม่พอใจที่ต้องตื่นเช้ามาก

items.stem: What does the woman say about the safety induction?
options: All who go onto the mudflats must attend, staff included.
Only the students are required to attend it.
It can be completed online before the visit.
It is held every morning before the low tide begins.
items.explanationTh: เธอบอกว่า "everyone who goes onto the flats has to attend" และ "not even for teaching staff" จึงต้องเข้าทุกคนรวมถึงอาจารย์ จัดในคืนแรก

items.stem: When will the booking be confirmed?
options: As soon as the man replies to the email.
Once the department has approved the cost.
On the evening the group arrives.
After the station has received a deposit.
items.explanationTh: เธอบอกว่าจะส่งการจองชั่วคราวก่อน และ "It only becomes confirmed once we receive a deposit" คือยืนยันเมื่อได้รับเงินมัดจำ

groups.instructionTh: ฟังการบรรยาย/ประกาศต่อไปนี้ แล้วตอบคำถาม 5 ข้อ (เนื้อหาจะเล่นเป็นเสียง)
groups.title: Safety briefing: organic chemistry practicals
groups.text:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the second-year organic chemistry practicals. Before anyone touches a flask, I need ten minutes of your undivided attention, because nothing I'm about to say is optional.

First, the basics. Lab coats stay buttoned, goggles stay over your eyes, not on your forehead and not around your neck, and long hair is tied back. If I see goggles anywhere other than over your eyes, you'll be asked to leave for the day, and the session will be recorded as missed.

Second, the fume cupboards. Each bench has one, and the airflow indicator on the front should sit in the green zone. If it drops into amber, finish the step you're on and then stop. If it reaches red, step back, pull the sash down and tell a demonstrator. Please don't try to fix it yourself. Last year somebody taped over an alarm because they found it annoying, and the entire floor had to be evacuated.

Third, waste. At the end of each row there are three containers: halogenated solvents, non-halogenated solvents and aqueous waste. Mixing them isn't just untidy. Certain combinations can heat up or give off gas. If you're not sure where something belongs, leave it in a labelled beaker and ask. A labelled beaker never hurt anybody.

Fourth, spills. Small spills on your own bench you can deal with using the kits under the sinks. Anything on the floor, anything on a person, or anything you can smell from more than a metre away is not a small spill. Call out, move away and let the staff handle it.

Finally, phones. I know you like to photograph your results for your notebooks, and that's fine, but phones stay in the clear plastic sleeves by the door, and you take them out only at the write-up tables. Gloves and touchscreens don't mix, and I've seen what a phone looks like after a bath in acetone.

Right. Any questions? No? Then find your bench number on the board and we'll begin.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of the talk?
options: To show students how to record their results.
To explain how to dispose of chemical waste.
To go over rules students must follow in the lab.
To describe an incident with a fume cupboard alarm.
items.explanationTh: ทั้งการบรรยายไล่กฎทีละข้อ (แว่นตา ตู้ดูดควัน ของเสีย การหก โทรศัพท์) และบอกว่า "nothing I'm about to say is optional" เรื่องของเสียและเหตุการณ์สัญญาณเตือนเป็นเพียงส่วนย่อย ไม่ใช่จุดประสงค์หลัก

items.stem: What will happen to a student who wears goggles on the forehead?
options: They will be given a formal verbal warning.
They will be sent out and marked as absent.
They will have to buy a new pair.
They will move to a different bench.
items.explanationTh: ผู้พูดบอกว่าถ้าแว่นไม่อยู่บนตา "you'll be asked to leave for the day, and the session will be recorded as missed"

items.stem: What should students do if the fume cupboard indicator reaches red?
options: Try to reset the airflow themselves.
Close the sash and inform a demonstrator.
Leave the floor by the nearest exit.
Complete the current step and then stop.
items.explanationTh: เมื่อถึงสีแดง ให้ "step back, pull the sash down and tell a demonstrator" ส่วน "finish the step you're on" เป็นวิธีปฏิบัติเมื่อเป็นสีเหลืองอำพัน (amber)

items.stem: Why does the speaker mention the alarm incident from last year?
options: To show that the alarms are often faulty.
To praise a student for acting quickly.

groups.title: Lecture: the Byzantine gold coin
groups.text:
Last week we looked at how the late Roman state paid its soldiers. Today I'd like to follow a single coin, the gold solidus, across roughly seven centuries, because its story tells us a surprising amount about Byzantine power.

The solidus was introduced in the early fourth century, and what made it remarkable was not its beauty but its stability. For about seven hundred years, its weight and gold content barely changed. Merchants well beyond the empire's borders accepted it without weighing or testing it, which is the ancient equivalent of a currency that everyone trusts at face value. Historians sometimes call it the dollar of the Middle Ages, though I'd treat that phrase with caution. It exaggerates the coin's reach, and it ignores the fact that most ordinary people in the empire rarely, if ever, held one. Everyday life ran on copper.

So why did stability matter so much? Largely because the state collected its taxes in gold and paid its army and officials in gold. As long as the coin held its value, that cycle held the empire together. When the cycle broke, so did confidence.

And break it did. In the eleventh century, under pressure from wars on several frontiers, emperors began quietly reducing the gold content. Within a few decades, a coin that had been almost pure was, in some issues, less than a quarter gold. What I find striking, and what I'd like you to think about for the seminar, is that this did not happen in a single desperate moment. The evidence from buried hoards suggests a gradual slide, each emperor issuing a slightly poorer coin than the last, perhaps assuming nobody would notice.

People did notice. Hoards from this period show owners deliberately keeping older, purer coins and spending the newer ones, a pattern any economist would recognise immediately. Eventually, a reform at the end of the century introduced a new gold coin, and the old solidus disappeared.

For the seminar, please read the two chapters on the hoard evidence and come prepared to argue one question: was debasement a cause of the empire's decline, or merely a symptom of it?

groups.title: Beyond the genetic script
groups.text:
For much of the twentieth century, the genome was pictured as a fixed instruction manual whose contents were ___1___ once and for all at conception. The sequence of DNA you inherited determined, more or less, what your cells could and could not do. Epigenetics ___2___ this picture considerably. The term refers to chemical modifications that alter how genes are expressed ___3___ changing the underlying sequence itself.

One of the best-studied of these modifications is DNA methylation, in which small chemical tags attach to particular sites and tend to ___4___ nearby genes, effectively switching them off. Crucially, such marks are not permanent. They can be added or removed in response to diet, stress and other environmental factors, ___5___ helps to explain why genetically identical twins often grow more different from each other as they age.

The most provocative claims in the field concern inheritance. Experiments on laboratory animals have suggested that some marks acquired by parents can be ___6___ to their offspring. ___7___, researchers urge caution in extending these findings to humans. Most marks are erased during the formation of egg and sperm cells, a process sometimes compared to wiping a whiteboard clean ___8___ a new lesson, and the few that appear to survive are extremely difficult to trace across human generations that may span several decades.

Popular accounts have not always ___9___ these limits. Headlines announcing that our grandparents' habits are "written into our genes" tend to overstate evidence that remains, for now, suggestive ___10___ conclusive. The more defensible conclusion is modest but still striking: our genes are less a fixed script than a score that can be performed in more than one way.

groups.title: In defence of the semicolon
groups.text:
Few punctuation marks provoke ___1___ disagreement as the semicolon. Some writers treat it as a sign of sophistication; others regard it as pretentious, a mark that ___2___ attention to the writer rather than to the idea being expressed.

The mark itself has a far longer ___3___ than many of its critics assume. It was popularised by a Venetian printer in the late fifteenth century, ___4___ wanted a pause longer than a comma but shorter than a full stop. For several centuries afterwards it was used generously, ___5___ in the long, carefully balanced sentences that were admired in essays and public speeches.

Its decline began when influential style guides started to ___6___ shorter sentences and plainer prose. A writer who had once linked two related clauses with a semicolon was now advised to split them into separate sentences, ___7___ sacrificing some of the logical connection between them. Newspapers, with their narrow columns and impatient readers, accelerated the trend, and by the late twentieth century many students were leaving school without ever having been taught how to use the mark at all.

Defenders argue that what was lost in this shift is precisely what made the semicolon valuable. A semicolon signals that two statements are grammatically independent ___8___ closely related in meaning, a nuance that neither a full stop nor the word "and" can quite ___9___. A full stop separates the ideas too sharply; "and" merely adds one to the other without saying how they are connected.

Whether the semicolon survives may depend less on grammar than on fashion. ___10___ writers come to value precision over speed once again, the humble mark may yet enjoy a modest revival.

groups.title: The logic of cooperation
groups.text:
Why do strangers cooperate? To an economist trained in classical game theory, the question is less trivial than it sounds. Consider the familiar scenario in which two players must each decide, without communicating, whether to cooperate or to defect. If both cooperate, both do reasonably well; if both defect, both do poorly; but a player who defects while the other cooperates does best of all, leaving the trusting partner with nothing. Analysed as a single encounter, the logic is bleak. Whatever the other player does, defecting yields a higher payoff, so rational players should defect, and both end up worse off than if they had trusted each other.

The picture changes, however, when the same players meet repeatedly. In a repeated game, today's choice casts a shadow over tomorrow. A player who defects now may gain in the short term but invites retaliation in every round that follows. Cooperation, in other words, can be sustained not by goodwill but by the prospect of future punishment. Theorists have shown that, provided players care sufficiently about future rounds, mutual cooperation can be an entirely rational outcome.

The economist Ingrid Solberg recently dramatised this insight in a classroom tournament at Harrowmere College. She invited her students to submit strategies, short computer programs that decided whether to cooperate or defect on the basis of the previous moves, and pitted each against every other over several hundred rounds. The winner was strikingly simple. It cooperated on the first move and thereafter copied whatever its opponent had done in the previous round. It never defected first, punished defection immediately, and forgave as soon as the opponent returned to cooperation. More elaborate entries, several of which tried to exploit naive opponents, tended to provoke cycles of retaliation that dragged down their own scores.

It would be easy to read too much into this result. Solberg herself cautioned that the winning strategy owed part of its success to the particular mix of entries; against a different population, it could well have been outscored. It is also vulnerable to error. If one player defects by mistake, through a misread signal or a slip of the finger, two copies of the strategy can become locked in an endless echo of mutual punishment. When Solberg reran the tournament with random errors added, a slightly more forgiving variant, which occasionally let a defection pass unanswered, came out on top.

Nonetheless, exercises of this kind have shifted the debate. They suggest that cooperation does not require altruism, central authority, or even much intelligence: it can emerge from simple rules applied consistently by agents who expect to meet again. That conclusion has since been applied, sometimes rather loosely, to subjects ranging from trade agreements to the behaviour of shoaling fish. The broader lesson is perhaps more modest. Whether cooperation flourishes depends less on the virtue of individuals than on the structure of their interactions, and above all on whether the future matters enough to discipline the present.

groups.title: When frozen ground lets go
groups.text:
Permafrost is defined not by what it contains but by its temperature: any ground that remains at or below zero degrees Celsius for at least two consecutive years qualifies, whether it consists of rock, sand or peat. Across the northern high latitudes, such ground underlies a large share of the land surface, in places to depths of several hundred metres. For most of human history it attracted little attention beyond the engineers who had to build on it. That has changed, because frozen ground turns out to be one of the largest stores of carbon on the planet.

The carbon consists of the remains of plants and animals that accumulated over tens of thousands of years and froze before microbes could break them down. As long as it stays frozen, it is effectively locked away. When it thaws, microbes resume their work, releasing carbon dioxide and, in waterlogged soils where oxygen is scarce, methane, a gas that traps far more heat over the short term. Because the Arctic is warming considerably faster than the global average, scientists worry about a feedback loop: thaw releases greenhouse gases, which cause further warming, which causes further thaw.

For years, most projections assumed that thaw would proceed gradually, creeping downward a few centimetres at a time as summers lengthened. Field researchers increasingly argue that this picture is incomplete. Where the ground contains large bodies of ice, thaw can be abrupt. As the ice melts, the surface collapses, forming pits, slumps and lakes in a process known as thermokarst. A hillside that looked stable one summer may, by the next, have slid away, exposing frozen soil several metres deep to the air at once. A team at the Tarvik Polar Institute estimates that, although abrupt thaw affects less than a fifth of the permafrost region, it could account for close to half of the carbon released from thawing ground this century. If so, models that treat thaw as a slow, even process may seriously understate the problem.

The uncertainty cuts both ways, however. Warmer conditions also allow shrubs and grasses to spread northward, and growing plants absorb carbon. Some of the lakes created by thermokarst eventually drain and fill with vegetation, which may partly offset earlier emissions. How these opposing processes balance out remains one of the most debated questions in climate research.

For the communities that live on permafrost, the debate is anything but abstract. Roads buckle, pipelines shift, and buildings whose foundations were designed for permanently frozen ground develop cracks as the soil beneath them softens. In one town surveyed by the Tarvik team, nearly a third of residential buildings showed structural damage linked to thaw. Engineers have responded with adaptations ranging from raised foundations to passive cooling pipes that draw winter cold down into the ground. These measures are effective but expensive, and they treat the symptoms rather than the cause. Ultimately, the fate of frozen ground, and of the people who depend on it, will be settled by decisions about emissions made far to the south.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความต่อไปนี้ แล้วตอบคำถาม 8 ข้อ
groups.title: Does language shape thought?
groups.text:
Does the language you speak shape the way you think? Few questions in the study of mind have swung so dramatically in and out of fashion. In its strongest form, sometimes called linguistic determinism, the idea holds that language sets the limits of thought: if your language lacks a word for something, you cannot conceive of it. Hardly anyone defends that version today. Speakers routinely grasp concepts their languages do not name, and translation, however imperfect, would be impossible if languages sealed their users inside separate mental worlds.

A weaker claim has proved far more durable. Linguistic relativity, as it is usually called, proposes not that language imprisons thought but that it nudges it, making certain distinctions habitual, easy and fast while leaving others available but effortful. The question then becomes an empirical one: can such effects be measured, and are they large enough to matter?

Colour has long been a favourite testing ground. Languages divide the spectrum differently; some use separate basic words for two shades of what English speakers simply call blue, much as English separates red from pink. In laboratory tasks, speakers of such languages are often slightly faster at telling apart two shades that straddle their linguistic boundary than two equally different shades that fall within the same category. The effect is real but small, measured in fractions of a second, and it tends to vanish when participants must repeat a string of numbers aloud while doing the task. This suggests that the advantage depends on silently naming the colours rather than on perceiving them differently.

Spatial language offers more striking evidence. Many languages describe location mainly in relation to the speaker's body: the cup is to the left of the plate. Others rely instead on fixed directions, closer to north and south: the cup is to the east of the plate. Researchers working with speakers of Kelari, a language that uses the second system almost exclusively, found that they kept track of compass directions with remarkable accuracy, even indoors and after being turned around several times. When asked to rebuild a row of objects after rotating 180 degrees, Kelari speakers preserved the objects' compass orientation, whereas speakers of body-based languages preserved their left-to-right order.

Sceptics point out that such differences need not originate in language at all. Communities that live in open landscapes and travel long distances may develop both the habit of tracking direction and the vocabulary to express it; language could be a symptom of culture rather than its cause. Disentangling the two is notoriously difficult, since researchers cannot randomly assign children to grow up speaking different languages.

What emerges is a more nuanced view than either the early enthusiasts or their later critics allowed. Language does not draw the boundaries of what we are able to think. It does, apparently, influence what we attend to, what we remember, and which distinctions we make without effort. Whether that amounts to a different way of seeing the world depends, perhaps, on how much weight one is prepared to give to habit.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความต่อไปนี้ แล้วตอบคำถาม 8 ข้อ
groups.title: Lean, fragile, resilient
groups.text:
For roughly four decades, the dominant philosophy in manufacturing could be summed up in a single word: lean. Inventory was regarded as waste, money tied up in parts sitting idle on shelves. The ideal factory held almost no stock, receiving components from suppliers only hours before they were needed. This "just-in-time" approach cut storage costs, exposed inefficiencies and allowed firms to respond quickly to shifts in demand. It also stretched supply chains across continents, as companies sought the cheapest possible supplier for every part, wherever it happened to be.

The weakness of the model is that it works superbly until it does not. A lean system has, by design, very little slack, and slack is precisely what absorbs shocks. When a single factory producing a critical component is shut by a flood, a fire or a port closure, there is no buffer of stock to fall back on, and production downstream can stop within days. Managers at Norvane, a mid-sized electronics assembler, discovered this when a fire at a distant plant halted deliveries of a small, inexpensive sensor. Norvane had no idea that the sensor came from a single site; its direct supplier had obtained it from a subcontractor two tiers further down the chain. Assembly lines worth millions of dollars stood idle for six weeks for want of a part costing less than a dollar.

A further complication is what analysts call the bullwhip effect. Small fluctuations in consumer demand tend to grow larger as they travel upstream. A retailer who notices a modest rise in sales orders a little extra to be safe; the wholesaler, seeing a larger order, adds its own margin; by the time the signal reaches the producer of raw materials, a ten per cent rise at the checkout may have become a fifty per cent surge in orders. When demand levels off, the whole chain is left holding surplus stock, and orders collapse just as dramatically. Notably, nobody in this sequence behaves foolishly. Each firm acts sensibly given what it can see; the trouble is that no one can see the whole chain.

In response, many firms now speak of resilience rather than efficiency. In practice this may mean holding larger stocks of critical parts, approving a second supplier for key components, or mapping the chain beyond the first tier so that hidden concentrations of risk come to light. Some companies now share sales data directly with their suppliers, reducing the guesswork that feeds the bullwhip.

None of these measures is free. Extra inventory ties up capital; second suppliers are often more expensive; mapping a network of thousands of firms demands time and a good deal of goodwill. The real challenge, therefore, is not to abandon lean thinking but to decide where its savings are worth the risk. A firm might happily run lean on generic parts that are available from many sources while keeping a deep buffer of anything that comes from a single site. Efficiency and resilience, in other words, are not so much opposites as competing priorities that must be weighed part by part.

groups.title: Can a theory always be rescued?
groups.text:
Ask a scientist what distinguishes science from other ways of knowing, and a common answer is that scientific claims can be tested. The most influential version of this view holds that a theory earns the label "scientific" not because it can be proved true, since no finite number of observations could ever do that, but because it could, in principle, be proved false. The claim that all swans are white can never be confirmed by any number of white swans, yet a single black swan refutes it. On this account, a good theory sticks its neck out: it forbids certain observations and stands ready to be abandoned if they occur.

The appeal of this criterion, usually called falsifiability, is obvious. It explains why claims that are compatible with every possible outcome, such as a horoscope so vague that it fits any week, strike us as unscientific. It also gives scientists a clear duty: rather than seeking confirmation, they should hunt for the observations most likely to sink their own theories.

Yet the criterion runs into difficulties as soon as one looks closely at how testing actually works. No theory is ever tested in isolation. To derive a prediction from a theory of planetary motion, for instance, one must also assume that the telescope is working properly, that the light has not been distorted on its way, that no unknown body is exerting its own pull, and so on. When the prediction fails, logic alone cannot tell us which of these assumptions to blame. The theory may be wrong, but so may any of the auxiliary assumptions that accompanied it. Faced with an awkward result, a scientist can always rescue a favoured theory by adjusting something else.

Historians of science point out that this is not merely a logical loophole: scientists have often done exactly this, and sometimes wisely. When a planet was observed to drift from its predicted orbit, astronomers did not discard their theory of gravitation; they proposed an unseen planet, and in one celebrated case it was subsequently found. The same strategy, applied to a different anomaly, led to a long search for another hidden planet that was never located; that deviation was eventually explained only by an entirely new theory of gravity. At the time, no rule could have told astronomers which response was the right one.

Does this mean that the demand for testability is empty? Not quite. What it suggests is that testing is a matter of judgement rather than mechanical procedure. A theory that is repeatedly rescued by new assumptions with no independent support begins to look suspicious; one whose rescues lead to fresh discoveries earns credibility. The question is not whether a theory can be saved, because it almost always can, but what the saving costs and whether it opens new lines of inquiry or merely shields the theory from criticism.

Some critics conclude that science is therefore less rational than its textbook image suggests. A more charitable reading is that rationality in science was never a matter of following an algorithm. It resembles the judgement of an experienced judge or engineer: constrained by evidence, answerable to colleagues and capable of error, yet far from arbitrary.

items.explanationTh: ประธาน "the present study" เป็นเอกพจน์ ปัจจุบันกาล กริยาต้องเติม -s เป็น measures

items.stem: So [[convincing]] [[the evidence was]] that the reviewers [[withdrew]] [[their]] objections.
items.explanationTh: เมื่อขึ้นต้นประโยคด้วย So + คุณศัพท์ ต้องสลับกริยาไว้หน้าประธาน คือ "So convincing was the evidence that..."

items.stem: The reforms [[were designed]] to reduce costs, [[to improve]] transparency [[and]] [[strengthening]] public confidence in the agency.
items.explanationTh: ต้องใช้โครงสร้างขนาน (parallel structure) to reduce, to improve และ (to) strengthen จึงใช้ strengthening ไม่ได้

groups.instructionTh: เลือกส่วนที่ขีดเส้นใต้ซึ่งผิดหลักไวยากรณ์ (มีเพียงหนึ่งส่วนในแต่ละประโยค)

items.stem: If the committee [[had received]] the report [[earlier]], [[it]] [[would make]] a decision before the end of last term.
items.explanationTh: เงื่อนไขแบบที่ 3 (If + had V3) ผลต้องเป็น would have + V3 จึงต้องเป็น "would have made" (ประโยคพูดถึงอดีต "last term" จึงต้องใช้ would have made)

items.stem: The new sampling method is [[considerably]] [[more cheaper]] than the conventional approach and [[requires]] [[less]] specialised equipment.
items.explanationTh: cheap เป็นคำพยางค์เดียว ขั้นกว่าคือ cheaper ห้ามใช้ more ซ้อน

items.stem: The students [[were]] [[responsible]] [[of]] collecting data [[from]] three provinces.
items.explanationTh: คำคุณศัพท์ responsible ใช้คู่กับบุพบท for (responsible for) ไม่ใช่ of

items.stem: [[The]] honesty is [[widely]] regarded as [[an essential]] quality [[in]] researchers.
items.explanationTh: honesty เป็นนามนามธรรมที่ใช้ในความหมายทั่วไป จึงไม่ต้องมี The นำหน้า

items.stem: The experiment [[showed]] that the compound remained [[stable]] at high temperatures, [[contrary]] to what earlier studies had [[predict]].
items.explanationTh: past perfect ต้องเป็น had + V3 จึงต้องเป็น "had predicted"

items.stem: The village [[where]] the anthropologist lived [[for]] two years [[has]] since been studied by scholars [[which]] work in several disciplines.
items.explanationTh: scholars เป็นคน relative pronoun จึงต้องเป็น who ไม่ใช่ which

items.stem: The final results [[will announce]] at a meeting [[that]] is scheduled [[for]] early [[next]] month.
items.explanationTh: ผลการวิจัยไม่ได้ประกาศเอง ต้องใช้ passive voice "will be announced"

items.stem: Instead of [[rely]] on a single source, historians [[are trained]] to compare [[accounts]] [[written]] by different observers.
items.explanationTh: หลังบุพบท (instead of) ต้องใช้ gerund จึงต้องเป็น "relying"

items.stem: More than two hundred bird species [[have been]] [[recorded]] in the area [[since]] the station [[has opened]] in 2009.
items.explanationTh: หลัง since ที่บอกจุดเริ่มต้นในอดีตพร้อมปีที่ชัดเจน ต้องใช้ past simple "opened" ไม่ใช่ present perfect

items.stem: The committee members [[expressed]] [[its]] concern [[that]] the deadline was [[unrealistic]].
items.explanationTh: ประธานคือ "The committee members" (พหูพจน์) สรรพนามต้องเป็น their ไม่ใช่ its

groups.instructionTh: เลือกส่วนที่ขีดเส้นใต้ซึ่งผิดหลักไวยากรณ์ (มีเพียงหนึ่งส่วนในแต่ละประโยค)

items.stem: The reviewers [[objected]] [[to]] the authors [[draw]] such broad conclusions [[from]] a small sample.
items.explanationTh: object to มี to เป็นบุพบท จึงต้องตามด้วย gerund คือ "objected to the authors drawing" ไม่ใช่ draw

items.stem: Not only [[the study was]] poorly designed, but [[its]] conclusions were [[also]] overstated [[by]] the press.
items.explanationTh: เมื่อขึ้นต้นด้วย Not only ต้องสลับกริยาช่วยไว้หน้าประธาน คือ "Not only was the study..."

items.stem: The participants [[were]] reluctant to discuss income and [[generally]] [[avoided]] [[to answer]] such questions.
items.explanationTh: avoid ตามด้วย gerund เสมอ จึงต้องเป็น "avoided answering"

items.stem: The two theories, [[though]] [[superficially]] similar, [[differ]] in the assumptions [[on which they rest on]].
items.explanationTh: บุพบท on ถูกใช้ซ้ำ เมื่อย้าย on ไปไว้หน้า which แล้ว ต้องตัด on ท้ายประโยคออก เป็น "on which they rest"

items.stem: Few laboratories [[were willing]] to attempt the technique, [[because of]] it was [[such]] a complicated procedure [[that]] training took months.
items.explanationTh: because of ตามด้วยคำนาม/วลีนาม แต่ที่นี่ตามด้วยประโยค (it was...) จึงต้องใช้ because

items.stem: The climate of the northern provinces [[is]] [[generally]] cooler than [[the southern provinces]], [[especially]] in December.
items.explanationTh: ต้องเปรียบเทียบสิ่งเดียวกัน คือภูมิอากาศกับภูมิอากาศ จึงต้องเป็น "that of the southern provinces"

items.stem: The museum [[has]] an [[impressive]] collection of coins, many of [[them]] date [[from]] the sixth century.
items.explanationTh: ประโยคหลังจุลภาคต้องเชื่อมด้วย relative pronoun "many of which" ถ้าใช้ them จะกลายเป็นสองประโยคเชื่อมกันด้วยจุลภาค (comma splice)

items.stem: Students [[interesting]] in the exchange programme [[should]] attend the briefing [[held]] [[on]] Thursday.
items.explanationTh: ต้องใช้ interested (รู้สึกสนใจ) เพื่อบรรยายความรู้สึกของนักศึกษา ส่วน interesting แปลว่าน่าสนใจ

items.stem: Hardly [[had]] the seminar [[begun]] [[than]] the power [[failed]].
items.explanationTh: โครงสร้าง "Hardly had ... when ..." ใช้ when ส่วน than ใช้กับ "No sooner had ... than ..."

items.stem: Researchers [[have long debated]] the extent [[which]] early experience [[shapes]] [[later]] behaviour.
items.explanationTh: สำนวน "the extent to which" ต้องมีบุพบท to หน้า which จึงต้องเป็น "to which"
